logical.name: Logical processors
logical.description: Number of logical processors (hardware threads) the operating system schedules work on. With simultaneous multithreading this exceeds the number of physical cores.

package.name: Processor packages
package.description: Number of physical processor packages (sockets) installed.

physical.name: Physical cores
physical.description: Number of physical execution cores, counted as distinct (package, core) pairs so that identically numbered cores in two different packages are never merged.

current.name: Current frequency
current.description: Clock frequency the operating system currently reports for this logical processor. Scaling, boost and power policies move it continuously, so it is the platform's latest figure rather than an instantaneous measurement of the silicon.

max.name: Maximum frequency
max.description: Maximum clock frequency the platform reports for this logical processor. On a hybrid CPU this differs between performance and efficiency cores. A governor or power-policy ceiling is never published here in its place.

package.name: Package temperature
package.description: Temperature the processor package reports for itself. It is the package's own sensor, never an average of the individual cores, and never one of the thermal limits the silicon is designed around.

logical.name: CPU usage
logical.description: Share of CPU time this logical processor spent doing work, measured since the previous sample. With simultaneous multithreading, two logical processors share one physical core.

total.name: CPU usage
total.description: Share of CPU time spent doing work across the whole machine, measured since the previous sample.

count.name: GPUs
count.description: Number of hardware graphics adapters PULSE inventoried. Software adapters such as Microsoft Basic Render Driver and WARP are not counted.

speed.name: Fan
speed.description: Speed the adapter's fan is turning at, in revolutions per minute. A fan control percentage is a duty cycle rather than a speed, and is never published in its place.

core.name: Core clock
core.description: Current graphics clock the driver reports. Boost behaviour and power policies move it continuously, so it is the platform's latest figure rather than an instantaneous measurement of the silicon.

memory.name: Memory clock
memory.description: Current video memory clock the driver reports.

free.name: Free VRAM
free.description: Dedicated video memory still available for allocation.

total.name: Total VRAM
total.description: Dedicated video memory installed on this adapter. System memory shared with an integrated GPU is deliberately not reported here.

percent.name: VRAM usage
percent.description: Share of dedicated video memory in use, computed from used and total bytes.

used.name: Used VRAM
used.description: Dedicated video memory currently in use across the whole system.

core.name: Temperature
core.description: Temperature of the graphics processor die, as its own sensor reports it.

hotspot.name: Hotspot
hotspot.description: Hottest point measured on the graphics processor package. A separate sensor from the die temperature, typically reading higher under load, and never derived from it.

memory.name: Memory temperature
memory.description: Temperature of the dedicated video memory, from its own sensor.

core.name: GPU usage
core.description: Share of the graphics engine's capacity in use, as the driver reports it.

available.name: Available memory
available.description: Physical memory that can be allocated without swapping.

total.name: Total memory
total.description: Installed physical memory usable by the operating system.

percent.name: Memory usage
percent.description: Share of physical memory in use, computed from used and total bytes.

used.name: Used memory
used.description: Physical memory in use, defined as total minus available.

count.name: Interfaces
count.description: Number of network interfaces PULSE monitors. The loopback interface is deliberately excluded: it always exists and only ever carries traffic that never left this machine.

up_count.name: Connected
up_count.description: How many of the monitored interfaces currently carry a link. An adapter that is enabled but has no cable, or a radio not associated with a network, is not counted.

receive_speed.name: Link RX
receive_speed.description: The inbound capacity of the link, as the driver negotiated it — not how much is flowing. A gauge rather than a fixed value because Wi-Fi and Ethernet both renegotiate.

transmit_speed.name: Link TX
transmit_speed.description: The outbound capacity of the link. Equal to the inbound figure on Ethernet; frequently different on Wi-Fi.

mtu.name: MTU
mtu.description: The largest payload this interface carries in a single frame. A configuration fact rather than a reading, so it is a state.

bytes_per_second.name: Download
bytes_per_second.description: Bytes arriving at this machine per second, derived from the operating system's cumulative counters between two samples. Receive means inbound, from this machine's point of view.

dropped_per_second.name: RX dropped
dropped_per_second.description: Inbound frames that arrived intact and were discarded anyway — a full buffer, or no protocol handler wanting them. This is a local counter and is not Internet packet loss, which PULSE does not measure.

errors_per_second.name: RX errors
errors_per_second.description: Inbound frames the interface rejected because something was wrong with them — a bad checksum, a framing error. A different counter from dropped frames, and a persistent non-zero rate usually means a cable or a driver problem.

packets_per_second.name: RX packets
packets_per_second.description: Packets arriving per second, unicast and non-unicast together. Zero is a real measurement: it means nothing arrived during the interval.

bytes_per_second.name: Upload
bytes_per_second.description: Bytes leaving this machine per second, derived from the operating system's cumulative counters between two samples. Transmit means outbound.

dropped_per_second.name: TX dropped
dropped_per_second.description: Outbound frames discarded before transmission, usually because a queue was full.

errors_per_second.name: TX errors
errors_per_second.description: Outbound frames the interface failed to transmit.

packets_per_second.name: TX packets
packets_per_second.description: Packets leaving per second, unicast and non-unicast together.

receive_rate.name: Wi-Fi RX rate
receive_rate.description: The inbound rate negotiated with the access point. A capacity, not traffic: a link negotiated at 400 Mbit/s carrying nothing still reports 400 Mbit/s.

transmit_rate.name: Wi-Fi TX rate
transmit_rate.description: The outbound rate negotiated with the access point. Frequently different from the inbound rate.

quality.name: Quality
quality.description: A 0–100 link quality figure, published only where the operating system computes one itself. It is never derived from the signal strength: every common dBm-to-percentage formula is arbitrary, and a number produced that way would look like a measurement while being a guess.

rssi.name: Signal
rssi.description: Received signal strength in dBm, as the radio reports it — a logarithmic scale where −40 is strong and −90 is barely usable. On a radio associated over several links, this is the strongest active link's reading; dBm values are never averaged together.

running.name: Running
running.description: How many processes are executing on a processor or queued and ready to. Nearly every process on an idle desktop is waiting instead — for a timer, for input, for a disk — so a small number here is normal and not a sign of an idle machine. Windows reports no process-level state, so this figure is unavailable there rather than fabricated.

total.name: Processes
total.description: How many processes exist on this machine right now, including the ones PULSE cannot read the details of. A process that is refused still exists and is still counted.

total.name: Threads
total.description: Every thread of every visible process, added up. Processes whose thread count could not be read contribute nothing rather than a guess, so on a machine full of protected processes this is an understatement rather than an invention.

total.name: Capacity
total.description: Total addressable capacity of the physical device. This is the whole device, not the sum of the filesystems on it.

count.name: Storage devices
count.description: Number of physical storage devices PULSE inventoried. Partitions, loop devices, RAM disks and device-mapper volumes are not counted as devices of their own.

available_spare.name: Available spare
available_spare.description: Share of the device's reserve of replacement blocks that remains. This is not free space on the filesystem and not unallocated capacity: a completely full drive normally still reports 100 % spare.

media_errors.name: Media errors
media_errors.description: Media and data integrity errors the controller has detected and counted over the device's life.

percentage_used.name: Used endurance
percentage_used.description: The controller's estimate of how much of the device's rated write endurance has been consumed. Reported exactly as the device states it, including values above 100 % once the rating has been exceeded, and never converted into a health score.

power_on_hours.name: Power-on hours
power_on_hours.description: Hours the device's controller has been powered on, as it counts them.

temperature.name: Temperature
temperature.description: The storage controller's composite temperature — a single figure the device derives from its own sensors, not one individual sensor and not any other component's reading.

unsafe_shutdowns.name: Unsafe shutdowns
unsafe_shutdowns.description: Times the device lost power without being told to shut down first.

bytes_per_second.name: Read
bytes_per_second.description: Bytes read from the device per second, derived from the operating system's cumulative counters between two samples.

iops.name: Read IOPS
iops.description: Read operations completing per second. Zero is a real measurement: it means no read completed during the interval.

latency.name: Read latency
latency.description: Mean time a read took, as the operating system observed it — queueing included, and measured from the host rather than inside the device. An interval in which no read completed has no latency at all, and reports none rather than zero.

bytes_per_second.name: Write
bytes_per_second.description: Bytes written to the device per second, derived from the operating system's cumulative counters between two samples.

iops.name: Write IOPS
iops.description: Write operations completing per second. Zero is a real measurement: it means no write completed during the interval.

latency.name: Write latency
latency.description: Mean time a write took, as the operating system observed it. An interval in which no write completed reports no value rather than zero.

available.name: Available
available.description: Space this user can actually write to. Lower than the free space on filesystems that keep a reserve for the superuser, which is deliberate: the reserve is not available to you.

total.name: Volume size
total.description: Total size of the filesystem. Several filesystems on one device do not add up to the device's capacity, and a filesystem may span devices.

used.name: Used
used.description: Space on the filesystem that holds data, defined as total minus free blocks. Used and available do not sum to the total on filesystems that reserve blocks for the superuser.

count.name: Volumes
count.description: Number of mounted filesystems PULSE inventoried. A filesystem reachable at several paths counts once; pseudo-filesystems such as proc and sysfs are not counted.

percent.name: Volume usage
percent.description: Share of the filesystem that holds data, computed from used and total bytes.

metrics.notReported: This machine does not report this metric.

guidance.checkShell: Check that GNOME Shell is running this session, then refresh.
guidance.standardWayland: Overlays still work as standard Wayland windows: click-through when locked, but the compositor decides their stacking.
guidance.discoverAtLogin: GNOME Shell 45 discovers new extensions only at login. After logging back in, enable it here.
guidance.installSteps: Install the extension with the command below, log out and back in once, then enable it.
guidance.extensionsOn: Turn user extensions back on (Extensions app, or gsettings set org.gnome.shell disable-user-extensions false).
guidance.newerCopyInstalled: A newer copy is installed. Log out and back in to load it.
guidance.reinstallNewer: This PULSE ships a newer bridge. Reinstall it with the command below, then log out and back in.
guidance.notGreeted: Running. It has not greeted this PULSE yet: extension versions before 2 never do; newer ones do as soon as PULSE starts.
guidance.enableIt: Enable it to keep overlays above other windows.
guidance.reinstallAfterError: Reinstall it, log out and back in. The error is also in journalctl --user -b /usr/bin/gnome-shell.
guidance.reinstallShipped: Reinstall the version this PULSE ships.

steps.installDetail: Copies it to ~/.local/share/gnome-shell/extensions/ — your account only, no sudo.
steps.updateDetail: v{{installed}} is installed; this PULSE ships v{{bundled}}.
steps.login: Log out and back in once
steps.loginDetail: GNOME Shell 45 loads extension code only at login.
steps.enableDetail: With the button here, or in GNOME’s Extensions app.
steps.connectedDetail: The running extension greeted this PULSE.
steps.notConnectedDetail: Versions from 2 greet PULSE as soon as it starts.

details.unlocks: Unlocks: overlays stay above the focused application (Mutter make_above), and the overlay shortcut works whichever application has focus — GNOME 45 has no global-shortcut portal. Click-through when locked is PULSE's own and works with or without the bridge.
details.safety: Safety: it only touches windows owned by the process holding PULSE's bus name and titled exactly PULSE Overlay :: <id>. No polling, no input interception, no files, no network.
details.troubleshooting: Troubleshooting: after installing or updating, log out and back in — GNOME loads extension code only at login. Its log: journalctl --user -b /usr/bin/gnome-shell | grep "PULSE overlay bridge". If GNOME Shell ever misbehaves at login, turn user extensions off from another session with gsettings set org.gnome.shell disable-user-extensions true.
details.limits: Limits: GNOME still places Wayland windows itself, so positions and multi-monitor placement stay the compositor's; drag an overlay once in Edit mode. Verified on GNOME 45 only.

page.subtitle: Widgets in their own small windows on the desktop — above other apps where the system allows, click-through when locked. A safe desktop window: PULSE never injects into games.

table.searchLabel: Search processes by name or PID

processes.note: CPU is a share of this machine's entire capacity, so one thread saturating one logical processor is a small percentage, and the column adds up to roughly what the system CPU gauge shows. Read and Write are the platform's per-process I/O counters (see the documentation for how Fedora and Windows differ). Rates are measured between two snapshots, so they appear only after a refresh. Click a process to inspect it; right-click (or Shift+F10) for actions. Every action targets that exact process instance, is confirmed when destructive, and never runs on its own. Command lines are deliberately not collected.
processes.groupedByName: Grouped by process name: PULSE could not read these processes’ executables, so two unrelated programs with the same name would be counted together.

inspector.stale: This process has exited, and its PID now belongs to a different process. PULSE will not act on it.
inspector.exited: Process exited. Nothing further can be done to it.
inspector.self: This is PULSE itself. Ending it will close this application.
inspector.kernelThread: A kernel thread runs inside the kernel: it has no executable, no package and cannot be controlled from PULSE.
inspector.replaced: The file this process started from has since been deleted or replaced on disk.
inspector.versionNote: Description, product and company are declared by the file itself and are not proof of anything; the signature is what Windows verified.
inspector.provenanceNote: Provenance is evidence, not a verdict: a package or a valid signature does not make a program safe, and their absence does not make it malicious.
inspector.suspendedByPulse: PULSE suspended this process during this session.
inspector.notApplicableKernel: Not applicable to a kernel thread
inspector.searchHint: Opens your browser on a web search for the program's name
inspector.virusTotalHint: Opens VirusTotal's page for this hash in your browser. The file is never uploaded.

cpu.title: CPU details
cpu.noProcessors: No individual logical processor is exposed on this machine.
cpu.note: One physical core can carry several logical processors, so usage is reported per logical processor. Frequencies are what the operating system reports. The package temperature is the processor's own sensor, never an average of its cores.
cpu.noMax: no maximum frequency is published for this processor

gpu.none: No hardware graphics adapter was detected. Software renderers are deliberately not counted as GPUs.
gpu.note: VRAM figures describe each adapter's dedicated video memory. System memory shared with an integrated GPU is not reported as VRAM. Hotspot and memory temperatures are separate sensors, never derived from the GPU temperature, and a fan speed is shown only when the driver reports genuine revolutions per minute.
gpu.vramKnownOnly: Installed VRAM is known; live usage needs a vendor driver this adapter does not provide.
gpu.perfUnavailableDefault: This adapter’s driver exposes no utilisation, video memory or clock figures.

storage.none: No physical storage device was inventoried. Loop devices, RAM disks and device-mapper volumes are deliberately not counted as disks.
storage.otherVolumesHint: Mounted filesystems PULSE could not tie to one of the disks above. They are listed separately rather than attributed to the wrong device.
storage.note: Throughput, IOPS and latency are measured between two samples, so they appear only after a refresh. A latency is the mean over operations that actually completed: an interval with none has no latency at all, and shows — rather than 0 ms. Used endurance and available spare are the controller's own standardised figures — available spare is the reserve of replacement blocks, not free space on a filesystem.
storage.waitingHint: Disk activity is the difference between two readings. Refresh to measure it.
storage.noHealthLog: This device reports no standardised health log.

network.none: No network interface was inventoried. The loopback interface is deliberately excluded: it always exists and only ever carries traffic that never left this machine.
network.virtualHint: Bridges, container links and other software interfaces. Collapsed so a machine running containers does not bury its real adapters — never removed.
network.note: Download is what arrives at this machine and Upload is what leaves it. Traffic is measured between two samples, so it appears only after a refresh. Link speeds are the capacity the driver negotiated, in bits per second — not how much is flowing, which is in bytes. Dropped frames are a local counter and are not Internet packet loss, which PULSE does not measure.
network.waitingHint: Traffic is the difference between two readings. Refresh to measure it.

live.title: Live system sample
live.reconcile: used + available = total, so the two figures above always reconcile.
